The river
has a clock.

A delay can lower a flood peak. It can also move one river straight into another river’s crest.

01 / The meeting

Put the days
together.

Rain, melting snow and ice helped flood Pittsburgh in January 1996. The two rivers crested unusually close together. Here is what their daily mean discharge records show. Height is flow per second; width is one day. NWS account ↗

The gauges are miles from the junction. The black Ohio outline is a separate record, not a fitted sum. Travel, side streams, storage, regulation and measurement uncertainty all sit in the gap.

A daily mean is neither the instantaneous crest nor water depth. These records cannot tell us the hour a wave reached the city. A flow wave’s speed is not the speed of an individual water particle.

02 / A deliberately simpler world

Move a river.
Keep its water.

Copy the two upstream records into 24-hour blocks. Keep their heights. Now move the orange strip in time. This is arithmetic, not a prediction of what a dam, forest or real river could do.

Dashed outline = original sum; k = thousand ft³/s. The tinted middle is the original 15-day excerpt. Water outside it is still drawn and counted. Blank space means no water from this excerpt, not an empty real river. No wrapping. No clipping. No hourly observations invented.

Make a prediction, then pull the orange strip. Watch the combined height—not just where the tallest orange block goes.

Translation moves a shape intact. Attenuation spreads its outflow through time. Both can conserve volume. Neither means water has disappeared.

The USACE Clark method separates these ideas when transforming excess rainfall into runoff. This little three-day averaging rule is not Clark, a routing model or a feasible intervention. Read the distinction ↗

Try to break the lesson

Matching peak dates
is not the whole story.

In March 1964, the two upstream maxima in our window are four days apart. Yet the Ohio’s daily maximum is the third-highest in this archive. Open the window: a second Monongahela crest overlaps the broad Allegheny wave. One peak date throws away that shape.

March 1964Upstream window maxima 4 days apart276,000Ohio daily peak · ft³/s
February 1966Upstream window maxima on the same day236,000Ohio daily peak · ft³/s

Across 37 confluences in Germany and Austria, Guse and colleagues found that superposition was not the dominant driver of flood severity at most sites. Tributary magnitude, timing and the site all mattered; daily data limit timing precision. That is a counterweight to our mechanism—not a Pittsburgh estimate. Read the study ↗

Same water.
Different meeting.

Sliding the strip proves that timing can change a peak. It cannot tell us how much timing caused a real flood. Keep the amount, the whole shape and the places in the picture.

Sources, calculation rules & the limits of these clocks
Where the records come from

USGS modern OGC API v1, daily mean discharge: parameter 00060, statistic 00003, ft³/s. Snapshot retrieved 29 September 2026. All three stations have exactly 16,071 unique dates from 1 January 1960 through 31 December 2003. All 48,213 records are approved. Estimated values: Natrona 29, Braddock 91, Sewickley 114. Source results were sorted by date and checked for duplicates, gaps and time-series identity. No gap filling or interpolation is used. The download preserves observation IDs, qualifiers, revision timestamps, series IDs and exact source query receipts.

A date is not a UTC timestamp

Station metadata say EST and “uses daylight savings: Y.” The API returns calendar dates without time offsets. Modern USGS daily means are described as local standard time in CAMELS-SPAT §2.3; an older 1968 USGS memo discusses 23/25-hour transition days. We preserve the supplied dates and do not claim to have resolved every historic clock convention. Model blocks are explicitly 86,400 seconds each. The January 1996 and December 1992 examples avoid daylight-saving transitions.

Exactly what the experiment does

The 15 daily means around the chosen date become flat 24-hour teaching blocks, including ordinary flow; no baseflow is subtracted. For integer shift d, the sum is A(t) + M(t − d). Optional spreading replaces M with [M(t) + M(t − 1) + M(t − 2)] / 3. Each excerpt is zero outside its own support only. We draw all support from day −6 through day 23; nothing wraps. Represented volume = sum of block flows × 86,400 seconds. It is volume assigned to the copied excerpt, not a reconstructed flood volume or observed hourly hydrograph. A missing or incomplete window disables the experiment.

What is not modeled

No channel hydraulics, inundation, backwater, reservoirs, lateral inflows, rating-curve uncertainty or feasible operating rules. Gauge peak lags are not estimated travel times. The optional averaging kernel illustrates spreading but is not USACE Clark: Clark transforms excess rainfall, with translation and storage; its standard linear reservoir relation has fixed parameters, while variable Clark allows a changing response. None is calibrated here. Flood prediction or design requires much more.

Gauge geography & measurement

Allegheny at Natrona · 03049500: approximately 11,410 mi² drainage area, 24.3 river miles upstream of the confluence. Monongahela at Braddock · 03085000: 7,337 mi², 11.2 miles upstream. Ohio at Sewickley · 03086000: approximately 19,500 mi², 13.3 miles downstream. The map shows the 1996 sites. The USGS station history places Sewickley’s earlier gauge 1.5 miles upstream until May 1981. Gauge sites and regulation were not constant across the archive. Discharge records are hydrometric estimates, often based on stage/discharge relationships; even unflagged values are not error-free. † marks the source’s explicit ESTIMATED qualifier.
